name: Owen's Defense
summary: Owen's Defense is a hypermodern flank system where Black fianchettoes the queen's bishop with 1...b6 and ...Bb7 to pressure e4 and the long diagonal.
intro: Owen's Defense begins 1.e4 b6, when Black fianchettoes the queen's bishop with ...Bb7 to train it on e4 and the long light diagonal, conceding the broad centre in true hypermodern style with the intention of striking at it later. A typical continuation is 2.d4 Bb7 3.Bd3 e6.
line: e4 b6 d4 Bb7 Bd3 e6

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: Black's whole idea is hypermodern: rather than occupy the centre with pawns, Black lets White build a big e4/d4 duo and undermines it from the flank with the b7-bishop, moves like ...e6 and ...d5 or ...c5, and piece pressure on the long diagonal. The bishop on b7 is the soul of the position.

White, for the price of a small space edge, enjoys a broad, mobile centre and easy development. If Black is passive the extra space can become a bind, so Black must generate timely central breaks and complete development before White clamps down.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: After 2.d4 Bb7 3.Bd3 White solidly defends e4 and prepares Nf3 and castling. Black continues ...e6 and typically strikes with ...d5 or ...c5, sometimes reaching structures that transpose to the French or a Queen's-Indian setup depending on how the centre is resolved.

White's most ambitious tries involve a big pawn centre with c4 or f3 and Nc3, aiming to overrun Black, while quieter setups simply develop and rely on the space edge. Black meets each by keeping the b7-bishop active and choosing the right central lever.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The defence is named after the Reverend John Owen, a strong nineteenth-century English amateur who championed the early ...b6. Long considered offbeat, it is sound at club level and periodically appears as a surprise weapon; its frequent transpositions to French and Queen's-Indian structures give it a respectable pedigree.

keyIdeas: The b7-bishop pressures e4 and the long diagonal
Black concedes the centre to strike at it later
Positions can transpose to French or Queen's-Indian setups
A sound but offbeat hypermodern surprise weapon

white: Build and defend a broad e4/d4 centre
Support e4 with Bd3 and Nc3 or f3
Develop naturally with Nf3 and castle short
Use the space edge to restrict Black's pieces
Meet ...d5 or ...c5 while keeping central control
black: Fianchetto with ...Bb7 to eye e4 and the long diagonal
Prepare central breaks with ...e6 then ...d5 or ...c5
Keep the b7-bishop active and unblocked
Aim for French or Queen's-Indian structures when favourable
